plan.rationale: Competitor, market, customer, and internal workers are required to determine what AMD, Broadcom, and Intel are doing with GPUs and what those moves imply for NVIDIA.

findings.statement: AMD offers the Instinct MI300X accelerator, based on the CDNA 3 architecture, with up to 192 GB of HBM3 memory for large language model training and inference. The MI300X was sampling to key customers starting in Q3 2023. AMD also offers the Instinct MI300A, described as the world's first APU accelerator for HPC and AI workloads, which was sampling to customers.

AMD's Instinct accelerator roadmap includes the MI325X accelerator, available in Q4 2024 with up to 288 GB of HBM3E memory. The MI350 series, based on the CDNA 4 architecture, is expected to be available in 2025. The MI400 series, based on the CDNA Next architecture, is expected to arrive in 2026 for inference and large-scale AI training.

AMD Instinct MI350X and MI355X GPUs are built on the CDNA 4 architecture with 288 GB of HBM3E memory and 8 TB/s memory bandwidth. The MI350X delivers peak FP16 performance of 4.6 PFLOPS and peak FP8 performance of 9.228 PFLOPS. These air-cooled GPUs integrate with prior-generation MI300X and MI325X infrastructure.

AMD offers the Instinct MI350P PCIe card as part of the MI350 Series for deploying generative and agentic AI within existing infrastructure. The product page lists 128 GPU compute units and 144 GB of HBM3E memory. AMD positions it for leadership operating expense and simplified deployment in data centers.

AMD provides ROCm, a full open-source, production-ready software stack compatible with a broad range of AMD GPUs. ROCm includes drivers, libraries, and developer tools for programming AMD GPUs and supports AI frameworks including PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX. Compatible hardware spans AMD Instinct GPUs, Radeon GPUs, and iGPUs in select Ryzen AI processors.

AMD: ROCm 7.14, released July 15, 2026, adds support for PyTorch 2.12 and JAX 0.10.0, and validates TensorFlow versions 2.21, 2.20, and 2.19.1. Transformer Engine v2.12 is validated for MI300A, MI300X, MI350X, and MI355X. The release introduces TheRock, AMD's automated open-source build and release system for ROCm.

AMD: ROCm 7.0, released September 16, 2025, provides hardware enablement for Instinct MI350X and MI355X and supports FP4, FP6, and FP8 precision formats. It includes day-0 support for PyTorch 2.7 and 2.8, TensorFlow 2.19.1, and JAX 0.6.x, along with AITER pre-optimized operators and AMD Quark production-ready models.

AMD offers AMD Inference Microservices (AIMs), described as a no licensing fee, open, standards-based enterprise-ready AI stack. AIMs is intended to simplify AI deployment and migration for generative and agentic AI workloads on AMD Instinct GPUs.

AMD's Data Center Segment customers consist primarily of hyperscale data centers, OEMs, ODMs, system integrators, and independent distributors in domestic and international markets. Large hyperscale customers, OEMs, and ODMs deployed AMD Instinct MI350X Series GPUs in 2025. Client and Gaming Segment customers include PC OEMs, independent distributors, AIBs, and game console manufacturers.

AMD Instinct MI300X accelerators have been adopted by customers and partners including Microsoft Azure, Meta, Dell Technologies, HPE, and Lenovo. These adoptions span cloud providers and OEMs deploying AMD AI accelerators in data centers.

AMD announced in November 2026 that Neysa is scaling AI infrastructure in India with AMD Instinct, expanding access to bare-metal AI infrastructure and accelerator choice for Indian enterprises. AMD also completed the acquisition of Taalas, a specialized AI inference silicon company, in November 2026.

AMD's Instinct line of accelerators has been adopted by major cloud providers and research organizations for running large AI models. In October 2025, AMD signed a chip-supply agreement with OpenAI for OpenAI's expanding data center network. AMD also entered a $1 billion agreement with the U.S. Department of Energy to supply chips for federal high-performance computing projects.
limitations: Supported by third-party sources only.

findings.statement: AMD's go-to-market model includes the AMD Partner Network with Build Partners (OEMs, ODMs, hosting providers, and add-in board partners), Distributors, Solution Providers, and Embedded Partners. Sell partners include solution providers, etailers, retailers, system builders, value-added resellers, and distributors.

AMD's internal estimated pricing for an MI350P-based server is $327,238.40 USD, as cited in AMD's Advancing AI 2026 materials from July 2026. This figure is used in per-concurrency throughput-per-dollar comparisons.

AMD states the Instinct MI355X GPU hardware cost is $1.48 per hour per GPU. At a typical operating point of 129 tokens per second per user, the MI355X delivers inference at $0.173 per million tokens with 2,378 tokens per second per GPU on 24 GPUs.

AMD Inference Microservices (AIMs) is offered with no licensing fee as an open, standards-based enterprise-ready AI stack. AMD also works with cloud providers such as Vultr, which offers cloud GPU and bare-metal servers advanced by AMD Instinct GPUs and AMD EPYC CPUs.

AMD offers the AMD Instinct GPU as a data center AI accelerator intended for AI training and inferencing workloads. AMD positions these accelerators across deployment options that include cloud, data center, edge, and AI PCs. The Instinct accelerator is combined with EPYC CPUs and networking products for rack-scale data center AI infrastructure.

AMD's data center computing portfolio includes GPUs, AI accelerators, DPUs, SmartNICs, FPGAs, and Adaptive SoCs. These products are intended to meet computing performance requirements for data centers, supercomputers, AI and machine learning data center environments, and cloud environments.
AMD offers AMD RyzenAI processors for AI PCs and workstations. These processors support local AI experiences and responsive performance for on-device agentic AI tasks.

AMD provides ROCm software as part of an open, standards-based software platform. The platform is designed to enable AMD AI hardware to be deployed broadly and easily, with support for leading frameworks, cloud providers, OEMs, ISVs, and ecosystem partners.

AMD targets cloud and enterprise customers, including the world's largest hyperscale computing companies, with data center AI systems. AMD seeks to deliver end-to-end data center AI infrastructure at scale with its ecosystem for cloud and enterprise deployment.
AMD markets and sells its products directly to OEMs and through authorized third-party distributors. This distribution model applies to AMD's data center and client computing products.
AMD addresses regulated and sovereign AI, hybrid AI, edge and embedded AI, and AI PC and workstation segments. Deployment options span cloud, data center, edge, and on-device environments.

AMD's enterprise go-to-market model emphasizes OEM go-to-market models, channel ecosystems, and enterprise infrastructure markets. AMD sells its products directly to OEMs and through authorized third-party distributors rather than exclusively through direct sales.
AMD offers AMD-based virtual machines in the cloud so customers can achieve performance and OPEX advantages. This represents a cloud consumption option for AMD GPU compute.

Broadcom offers custom AI accelerators, described as application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) or XPUs, co-designed with large hyperscale customers. Broadcom does not sell its own branded AI chip; instead it partners with hyperscalers to design bespoke chips and manages manufacturing relationships and packaging. These accelerators support AI training and inference workloads.
limitations: Supported by third-party sources only.

findings.statement: Broadcom: Reported Broadcom custom AI silicon customers include Google, for whom Broadcom helped design Tensor Processing Units, as well as Meta. ByteDance is reported as a third customer. A fourth hyperscaler customer was qualified in FQ3 with over $10 billion in AI rack orders based on Broadcom XPUs. Separately, OpenAI is collaborating with Broadcom on co-designed inference-optimized chips and systems.
limitations: Supported by third-party sources only.

findings.statement: Broadcom offers Ethernet-based AI networking chips and Ethernet solutions for AI cluster scale-up and scale-out. Through its OpenAI collaboration, Broadcom supplies Ethernet networking alongside accelerators, with systems planned for deployment starting in the second half of 2026 and completion by end of 2029.
limitations: Supported by third-party sources only.

findings.statement: Broadcom: Cloud and hyperscale customers using Broadcom AI silicon or networking include Google, Meta, ByteDance (reported), an unnamed fourth hyperscaler, and OpenAI. Broadcom has indicated that four hyperscaler customers are each racing toward 1 million XPU clusters by the end of 2027. The supplied evidence does not specify the geographic markets (Americas, Asia, Europe) for these customers.
limitations: Supported by third-party sources only.

findings.statement: Intel Corp: Intel offers Gaudi AI accelerators and Gaudi software designed for data center training and inference to bring compute advantages and choice to data center workloads.
Intel Corp: Intel offers Data Center GPU Flex Series for virtual desktop infrastructure, media processing, and visual AI workloads.
Intel Corp: Intel offers Arc Pro B-Series GPU for workstation performance to run larger models and process richer data.
Intel Corp: Intel Xeon 6, Xeon 6+, and Xeon CPU Max processors are positioned for data center, network, edge, and workstation workloads.
Intel Corp: Intel Arc Graphics are engineered for immersive gameplay, fast content creation, and easy-to-use AI capabilities.
Intel Corp: Intel Arc G-Series processors target handheld gaming with smooth gameplay at high settings, AI-powered XeSS 3, and ray tracing.
Intel Corp: Intel Arc A750 Graphics is part of Intel's Arc dedicated graphics family for client systems.
Intel Corp: Intel oneAPI is an open, unified cross-architecture programming model supporting CPUs and accelerator architectures including GPUs and FPGAs.
Intel Corp: Intel oneAPI includes the DPC++ Compatibility Tool for CUDA-to-SYCL code migration, enabling developers to port CUDA applications.
Intel Corp: Intel oneAPI provides AI tools, optimized frameworks, and the OpenVINO toolkit, including oneDNN and PyTorch optimizations for Intel Core Ultra processors and Arc GPUs.
Intel Corp: Intel released oneAPI 2025.0 tools with a standalone oneAPI HPC Toolkit and an AI Tools Selector for OpenVINO Toolkit and Gaudi AI accelerator packages.
Intel Corp: Intel's Edge AI Portfolio combines OpenVINO for model inference, Geti platform for vision AI training, DL Streamer, and oneAPI toolkit for edge AI solutions.
Intel Corp: Intel oneAPI offers a Unified Runtime and Codeplay plug-ins for cross-vendor GPU support.
Intel Corp: Intel Xeon 6787P (2S) delivers 4x throughput on Speech Recognition (OpenAI Whisper) and 2.2x throughput on Computer Vision (RetinaNet) in MLPerf v5.1 inference.
Intel Corp: Intel Xeon processors include built-in Intel AMX acceleration for higher precision ML/DL workloads.
Intel Corp: Intel Xeon 6 processors with P-cores include Intel AMX and AVX-512 in every core, with AMX supporting INT8, BF16, and FP16 data types.

## TheRock Reaches Production[#](#therock-reaches-production "Link to this heading")

This release marks a significant milestone with the first official release of TheRock, AMD’s new automated, open-source build and release system for the ROCm software stack. The preview release train spanning versions 7.9 through 7.13 is complete, and ROCm 7.14 marks the start of our future production releases. Users on 7.2 and older are encouraged to migrate and follow the transition guide on [ROCm docs](https://rocm.docs.amd.com/en/docs-7.14.0/about/transition-guide-TheRock.html). TheRock packages the foundational components needed to run high-performance workloads on AMD GPUs, streamlining how ROCm is built and delivered going forward. TheRock introduces ROCm Core SDK, a base installation containing the essential components most users need, with optional expansion SDKs available for specialized domains including HPC, computer vision (ROCm-CV), data science (ROCm-DS), and life sciences (ROCm-LS). Built on a unified, pure-CMake build system, TheRock provides stable nightly releases with support for multiple Linux distributions and Windows. The open-source nature of TheRock accelerates adoption through public PRs, transparent CI pipelines, and code developed directly in public GitHub repositories. This results in a faster, continuous release cycle with improved quality and stability, reliable validation, and a smooth out-of-box experience.

### Market position
By the mid-2020s, AMD had become a major player in data center and AI computing while remaining a leading supplier of processors for personal computers and gaming devices. The company focuses on designing flexible chips that power everything from [laptops](/technology/laptop-computer) to large-scale AI systems.
This article was most recently revised and updated by [The Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica](/money/author/The-Editors-of-Encyclopaedia-Britannica/4419)

By the mid-2020s, as demand for [artificial intelligence](/science/history-of-artificial-intelligence) grew rapidly, AMD spent heavily to develop high-performance graphics processors and specialized chips for AI training and use in data centers. Its Instinct line of accelerators—chips designed to perform complex calculations faster than conventional processors—has been adopted by major cloud providers and research organizations for running large AI models, giving AMD a foothold in a market long dominated by **[NVIDIA](/money/NVIDIA-Corporation)** (NVDA).
### Partnership with OpenAI
In October 2025, AMD signed a chip-supply agreement with [OpenAI](/money/OpenAI), the company best known for developing the ChatGPT chatbot. Under the deal, AMD is to supply chips for OpenAI’s expanding network of data centers, which run the large computer systems needed to train and operate its AI models.

In 2022, AMD acquired Xilinx, a maker of programmable chips used in devices that require flexibility and real-time processing, such as cars, telecommunications equipment, and industrial systems. The $49 billion deal, the largest in AMD’s history, brought in technology that allows chips to be reconfigured after manufacturing, giving customers more control over performance and power use. It also expanded AMD’s presence in areas such as automotive electronics, communications, and data center infrastructure, extending its reach beyond traditional [central processing units](/technology/central-processing-unit) (CPUs) and [graphics processors](/technology/graphics-processing-unit).

# 7 Takeaways from AMD Advancing AI 2026 to Guide Your 2027 Infrastructure Plan

Aug 04, 2026

![Large event banner reads ](/content/dam/amd/en/images/blogs/designs/5210600-aai-data-center-insights.jpg)

Enterprise AI infrastructure planning is changing shape as organizations start shifting more from chatbot-style AI to agentic AI. An AI agent requires a new conversation because it doesn’t just generate a response — it plans, calls tools, queries databases, checks permissions, retrieves memory, and loops, often triggering other agents along the way. Each of those steps still runs on general-purpose compute, which shifts demand across CPU, GPU, networking, and orchestration software at the same time. This forces IT leaders to plan against a new set of criteria. Advancing AI 2026 was where AMD laid out its answer to this shift in detail.

Below are the 7 key takeaways from the event that enterprises should keep in mind when having 2027 infrastructure planning discussions.

### Start With Your Usage Model, Not a Spec Sheet

The first question to answer is not which GPU has the best peak performance, it’s “how does my organization actually use AI?” How many users, how many agents, which models, and how much data needs to stay on-premises for latency or sovereignty reasons? That usage model determines which compute tier you need, in what ratio, and where it should sit.

### Consider the CPU-GPU Ratio Before You Plan the GPU Count

The CPU isn't a supporting actor to the GPU story anymore. In an agentic workload, it's doing real work of its own, and that changes the order in which you should plan. For years, GPU capacity dominated AI infrastructure planning, with the CPU cast as a supporting host node. An agent's workflow breaks that assumption: every plan-call-query-check-retrieve-loop cycle still runs on general-purpose compute, and that workflow splits across distinct profiles that each lean on the CPU differently.

Agent orchestration and sandboxing benefit from CPUs built for that pattern. Host nodes that keep GPU clusters fed during reasoning and inference need a different profile. However, general-purpose enterprise applications (ERP, CRM, the databases agents query to get work done) still need to run somewhere. Planning around a single CPU standard risks under-provisioning at least one of those needs.

At Advancing AI 2026, AMD announced the latest 6th Generation [AMD EPYC™ 9006 Series Server CPUs](/en/products/processors/server/epyc/9006-series.html), the broadest server CPU portfolio built for agentic AI1, spanning cloud, enterprise, general-purpose and HPC workloads. As agent sandboxes, the generation runs the agents, coordinating concurrent agents and executing tasks; as AI host nodes, it keeps accelerators fed with speed and memory bandwidth; as general-purpose servers, it runs business-critical applications and AI support tasks enterprises depend on every day, with enhanced energy efficiency.

The practical implication: size your CPU layer to the workflow first, then size the GPU layer to the model. Getting that order backward is how enterprises end up with GPU clusters that are starved by their own host nodes.

### Match the GPU to Your Buying Scenario

Once you know your usage model and CPU ratio, the GPU decision narrows to the question of which buying scenario you're actually in — not which spec sheet looks best.

To help customers right-size their infrastructure, the new [AMD Instinct™ MI400 Series](/en/products/accelerators/instinct/mi400.html) GPUs are split into three products, positioned for three different buying scenarios, rather than one GPU sold for every use case. The AMD Instinct MI455X GPU is built for frontier-scale training and inference, backed by 432 GB of HBM4 memory and 3D chip-stack packaging. The AMD Instinct MI430X GPU (already running in exascale supercomputers at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and France's Jean Zay), targets HPC and sovereign AI workloads that need high-precision scientific computing rather than raw AI throughput. # Win on TCO: How AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs Achieve Cost-Competitive Distributed Inference Through SGLang with MoRI

May 27, 2026

![Abstract illustration with glowing blue lines](/content/dam/amd/en/images/abstract/3987700-confidential-ai-sev.jpg)

As large-scale LLM inference increasingly relies on multi-node disaggregated serving with wide Expert Parallelism (EP), the critical question for infrastructure teams is no longer "which GPU is fastest" but **"which platform delivers the lowest cost per token at production interactivity levels."**

Using [SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang) with AMD's [MoRI](https://github.com/ROCm/mori) communication library on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, we demonstrate that AMD achieves **competitive - and at key operating points, superior - Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)** compared to NVIDIA B200 running Dynamo + TRT-LLM on DeepSeek-R1 disaggregated inference. These results are validated by [InferenceX](https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/)™, SemiAnalysis's open-source continuous benchmark platform that tests across hundreds of GPUs with a live dashboard.

This post describes what we have achieved, how we achieve it, and our future plans.

![Figure 1: InferenceX TCO  Calculator— AMD Instinct™ MI355X and B200 configurations](/content/dam/amd/en/images/blogs/designs/technical-blogs/mori-distributed-inference/image1_tco-calculator.png)

Figure 1: InferenceX TCO Calculator— AMD Instinct™ MI355X and B200 configurations

## Results at a Glance

At the typical operating point representative of production coding assistants and interactive chatbots - e.g. **129 tok/s/user** interactivity - we observe the following:

* **AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs (MoRI SGLang MTP)**: **$0.173** per million tokens, **2,378** tok/s/GPU (achieved on 24 GPUs)
* **NVIDIA B200 (Dynamo TRT-LLM MTP)**: $0.178 per million tokens, **3,128** tok/s/GPU (achieved on 28 GPUs)
* **NVIDIA B200 (Dynamo SGLang MTP)**: $0.284 per million tokens, **1,945** tok/s/GPU (achieved on 48 GPUs)

The MI355X GPUs delivers **2.9% lower cost** than B200 TRT-LLM, **39% lower cost** than B200 SGLang, and **1.22× higher throughput** per GPU than B200 SGLang - winning on both cost and performance simultaneously.

![Figure 2: InferenceX Performance pareto curve — throughput vs interactivity for AMD Instinct™ MI355X MoRI SGLang vs B200 Dynamo SGLang](/content/dam/amd/en/images/blogs/designs/technical-blogs/mori-distributed-inference/image2_perf-pareto.png)

## Key Optimization Details

#### How MoRI quantized all2all dispatch/combine benefits expert parallelism

**Hybrid FP4/FP8 quantized all-to-all**

In expert-parallel MoE inference, each token must be dispatched to the top-k selected experts via dispatch and combine communication primitives. For DeepSeek-R1 with a hidden dimension of 7,168 and top-8 expert routing, BF16 communication volume is significantly higher than that of FP8 and FP4 quantized communication.

The key insight is that on-the-fly MXFP4 quantization of dispatch will bring faster transmission with accuracy lossless. Similarly, expert outputs (combine phase) tolerate FP8 quantization without meaningful accuracy loss.

SANTA CLARA, Calif., Aug. 19, 2024 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- [AMD](http://www.amd.com/ "AMD") (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced the signing of a definitive agreement to acquire [ZT Systems](https://ztsystems.com/ "ZT Systems"), a leading provider of AI infrastructure for the world’s largest hyperscale computing companies. The strategic transaction marks the next major step in AMD’s AI strategy to deliver leadership AI training and inferencing solutions based on innovating across silicon, software and systems. ZT Systems’ extensive experience designing and optimizing cloud computing solutions will also help cloud and enterprise customers significantly accelerate the deployment of AMD-powered AI infrastructure at scale.

AMD has agreed to acquire ZT Systems in a cash and stock transaction valued at $4.9 billion, inclusive of a contingent payment of up to $400 million based on certain post-closing milestones. AMD expects the transaction to be accretive on a non-GAAP basis by the end of 2025.

“Our acquisition of ZT Systems is the next major step in our long-term AI strategy to deliver leadership training and inferencing solutions that can be rapidly deployed at scale across cloud and enterprise customers,” said AMD Chair and CEO [Dr. Lisa Su](https://www.amd.com/en/corporate/leadership/lisa-su.html "Dr. Lisa Su"). “ZT adds world-class systems design and rack-scale solutions expertise that will significantly strengthen our data center AI systems and customer enablement capabilities. This acquisition also builds on the investments we have made to accelerate our AI hardware and software roadmaps. Combining our high-performance Instinct AI accelerator, EPYC CPU, and networking product portfolios with ZT Systems’ industry-leading data center systems expertise will enable AMD to deliver end-to-end data center AI infrastructure at scale with our ecosystem of OEM and ODM partners.”

Headquartered in Secaucus, New Jersey, ZT Systems has more than 15 years of experience designing and deploying data center AI compute and storage infrastructure at scale for the largest global cloud companies. ZT Systems’ design, integration, manufacturing and deployment capabilities have made them one of the leading providers of AI training and inference infrastructure.

“We are excited to join AMD and together play an even larger role designing the AI infrastructure that is defining the future of computing,” said Frank Zhang, CEO of ZT Systems. “For almost 30 years we have evolved our business to become a leading provider of critical computing and storage infrastructure for the world’s largest cloud companies. AMD shares our vision for the important role our technology and our people play designing and building the computing infrastructure powering the largest data centers in the world.”

Following transaction close, ZT Systems will join the AMD Data Center Solutions Business Group. # AMD to Significantly Expand Data Center AI Systems Capabilities with Acquisition of Hyperscale Solutions Provider ZT Systems

![Press Image](/content/dam/amd/en/images/pr/corporate-3.jpg)

*— Strategic acquisition to provide AMD with industry-leading systems expertise to accelerate deployment of optimized rack-scale solutions addressing $400 billion data center AI accelerator opportunity in 2027 —*

* ZT Systems, a leading provider of AI and general purpose compute infrastructure for the world’s largest hyperscale providers, brings extensive AI systems expertise that complements AMD silicon and software capabilities
* Addition of world-class design and customer enablement teams to accelerate deployment of AMD AI rack scale systems with cloud and enterprise customers
* AMD to seek strategic partner to acquire ZT Systems’ industry-leading manufacturing business
* Transaction expected to be accretive on a non-GAAP basis by the end of 2025

SANTA CLARA, Calif., Aug. 19, 2024 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- [AMD](http://www.amd.com/ "AMD") (NASDAQ: AMD) today announced the signing of a definitive agreement to acquire [ZT Systems](https://ztsystems.com/ "ZT Systems"), a leading provider of AI infrastructure for the world’s largest hyperscale computing companies. The strategic transaction marks the next major step in AMD’s AI strategy to deliver leadership AI training and inferencing solutions based on innovating across silicon, software and systems. ZT Systems’ extensive experience designing and optimizing cloud computing solutions will also help cloud and enterprise customers significantly accelerate the deployment of AMD-powered AI infrastructure at scale.

AMD has agreed to acquire ZT Systems in a cash and stock transaction valued at $4.9 billion, inclusive of a contingent payment of up to $400 million based on certain post-closing milestones. AMD expects the transaction to be accretive on a non-GAAP basis by the end of 2025.

“Our acquisition of ZT Systems is the next major step in our long-term AI strategy to deliver leadership training and inferencing solutions that can be rapidly deployed at scale across cloud and enterprise customers,” said AMD Chair and CEO [Dr. Lisa Su](https://www.amd.com/en/corporate/leadership/lisa-su.html "Dr. Lisa Su"). “ZT adds world-class systems design and rack-scale solutions expertise that will significantly strengthen our data center AI systems and customer enablement capabilities. This acquisition also builds on the investments we have made to accelerate our AI hardware and software roadmaps. Combining our high-performance Instinct AI accelerator, EPYC CPU, and networking product portfolios with ZT Systems’ industry-leading data center systems expertise will enable AMD to deliver end-to-end data center AI infrastructure at scale with our ecosystem of OEM and ODM partners.”

Headquartered in Secaucus, New Jersey, ZT Systems has more than 15 years of experience designing and deploying data center AI compute and storage infrastructure at scale for the largest global cloud companies. ZT Systems’ design, integration, manufacturing and deployment capabilities have made them one of the leading providers of AI training and inference infrastructure.

“We are excited to join AMD and together play an even larger role designing the AI infrastructure that is defining the future of computing,” said Frank Zhang, CEO of ZT Systems. “For almost 30 years we have evolved our business to become a leading provider of critical computing and storage infrastructure for the world’s largest cloud companies. AMD shares our vision for the important role our technology and our people play designing and building the computing infrastructure powering the largest data centers in the world.”

Following transaction close, ZT Systems will join the AMD Data Center Solutions Business Group. evidence.page_text:
The logic Nvidia appears to be betting on is straightforward. If a hyperscaler’s engineers are trained on, and dependent on, tools hosted through Hugging Face, then switching the underlying chip becomes a much bigger project than swapping a GPU order. Owning the place where models get built, shared and fine-tuned gives Nvidia leverage that doesn’t show up on a spec sheet and doesn’t require winning every hardware bake-off against a Broadcom-designed chip.
Broadcom’s Growing Roster of Custom AI Chip Customers
Broadcom’s custom silicon relationships have been reported across multiple hyperscalers over the past several years, most prominently in the design of Google’s Tensor Processing Units. That relationship alone has made Broadcom’s AI revenue a line item investors watch closely on every earnings call. Other reported design partnerships extend to additional large cloud and AI companies exploring their own accelerators rather than buying exclusively from Nvidia.
This is the same competitive pressure that has pushed
Microsoft to develop its Maia AI accelerators

. Its biggest customers, the hyperscale cloud providers, have spent years funding their own alternatives to Nvidia hardware, and Broadcom has become the company most of them call when they want a custom AI accelerator built to their own specifications rather than Nvidia’s general-purpose GPU roadmap. Broadcom doesn’t design its own competing chip brand the way AMD does. Instead, it partners with hyperscalers to co-design application-specific integrated circuits, then handles the manufacturing relationships and packaging, taking a cut of a market Nvidia would rather keep buying GPUs into.
That business model matters because it doesn’t require any single customer to publicly declare independence from Nvidia. A hyperscaler can keep buying Nvidia GPUs for general workloads while quietly shifting a growing share of training and inference to a custom chip designed with Broadcom. Analysis from Jon Peddie Research, a firm that tracks GPU and graphics market share, has flagged the Hugging Face acquisition as part of a broader pattern of Nvidia extending its reach up the software stack at the same moment custom silicon programs are maturing on the hardware side.

The clearest contrast between the two companies is their business model. NVIDIA generates the bulk of its revenue from GPU-based accelerated computing, while Broadcom blends semiconductors with a large software segment, creating a more diversified income stream. This diversification historically provides Broadcom with some ballast when semiconductor demand softens, though its AI exposure is increasingly concentrated among a handful of hyperscale customers.
On growth drivers, NVIDIA's momentum is tied to broad-based AI infrastructure demand and its dominant software ecosystem, whereas Broadcom's growth leans on custom accelerator programs and AI networking, which can be lumpy depending on individual customer commitments. In terms of recent momentum, Broadcom has posted faster share-price appreciation over the trailing year, but NVIDIA's more consistent earnings power and higher margins remain a point of strength.

Broadcom operates through two main segments: semiconductor solutions and infrastructure software, the latter built around its VMware acquisition. This structure differentiates [AVGO](https://tickeron.com/ticker/AVGO/) from pure-play chipmakers by adding recurring software revenue. The company's AI growth has been driven primarily by custom AI accelerators (also referred to as ASICs, or application-specific integrated circuits, and XPUs) designed for large hyperscale customers, along with Ethernet-based AI networking chips. The logic Nvidia appears to be betting on is straightforward. If a hyperscaler’s engineers are trained on, and dependent on, tools hosted through Hugging Face, then switching the underlying chip becomes a much bigger project than swapping a GPU order. Owning the place where models get built, shared and fine-tuned gives Nvidia leverage that doesn’t show up on a spec sheet and doesn’t require winning every hardware bake-off against a Broadcom-designed chip.
Broadcom’s Growing Roster of Custom AI Chip Customers
Broadcom’s custom silicon relationships have been reported across multiple hyperscalers over the past several years, most prominently in the design of Google’s Tensor Processing Units. That relationship alone has made Broadcom’s AI revenue a line item investors watch closely on every earnings call. Other reported design partnerships extend to additional large cloud and AI companies exploring their own accelerators rather than buying exclusively from Nvidia.
This is the same competitive pressure that has pushed
Microsoft to develop its Maia AI accelerators

. Its biggest customers, the hyperscale cloud providers, have spent years funding their own alternatives to Nvidia hardware, and Broadcom has become the company most of them call when they want a custom AI accelerator built to their own specifications rather than Nvidia’s general-purpose GPU roadmap. Broadcom doesn’t design its own competing chip brand the way AMD does. Instead, it partners with hyperscalers to co-design application-specific integrated circuits, then handles the manufacturing relationships and packaging, taking a cut of a market Nvidia would rather keep buying GPUs into.
That business model matters because it doesn’t require any single customer to publicly declare independence from Nvidia. A hyperscaler can keep buying Nvidia GPUs for general workloads while quietly shifting a growing share of training and inference to a custom chip designed with Broadcom. Analysis from Jon Peddie Research, a firm that tracks GPU and graphics market share, has flagged the Hugging Face acquisition as part of a broader pattern of Nvidia extending its reach up the software stack at the same moment custom silicon programs are maturing on the hardware side.

Broadcom has spent the past three years quietly building a custom AI
chip business

# Develop and Scale Your Code with Confidence

##### Highly productive development stack for AI and open, accelerated computing.

[Get the Toolkits](/content/www/us/en/developer/tools/oneapi/toolkits.html)

[About oneAPI](/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/oneapi-what-is-it.html) | [What's New](/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/news/oneapi-news-updates.html)

### Performance and Productivity: Scalable Hybrid Parallelism

#### Optimized AI from data center to PC. Real-time image processing. Get the latest developer tools from Intel now.

* Maximize AI PC inference capabilities from large language models (LLM) to image generation with Intel® oneAPI Deep Neural Network Library (oneDNN) and PyTorch optimizations for Intel® Core™ Ultra processors (series 2) and Intel® Arc™ GPUs.
* Efficiently handle complex models and large datasets in AI inference workflows with oneDNN optimizations for Intel® Xeon® 6 processors with P-cores. 
* Optimize performance on client GPUs and NPUs from Intel with new analysis tool features in Intel® VTune™ Profiler.
* Achieve real-time processing and display on a broader array of imaging formats through enhanced SYCL\* interoperability with Vulkan\* and Microsoft DirectX\* 12 APIs.
* Optimize GPU offload performance and flexibility for data-intensive applications with new OpenMP\* 6.0 features in the Intel® oneAPI DPC++/C++ Compiler. 
* Enhance efficiency for parallel computing and complex data structures with new Fortran 2023 features in the Intel® Fortran Compiler.
* Experience improved compatibility and application performance for hybrid parallelism with message passing interface MPI support and newly extended multithreading capabilities in the Intel® MPI Library.

[Explore Toolkits](/content/www/us/en/developer/tools/oneapi/toolkits.html) | [Stand-Alone Tools](/content/www/us/en/developer/tools/oneapi/components.html)

* [What Is oneAPI](#tab-blade-1-0)
* [Open Industry Initiative](#tab-blade-1-1)
* [Tools Powered by oneAPI](#tab-blade-1-2)

## A Vision of Developer Freedom for the Future of Accelerated Compute

oneAPI provides a comprehensive set of libraries, open source repositories, SYCL-based C++ language extensions, and optimized reference implementations to accelerate the following goals:

* Define a common, unified, and open multiarchitecture and multivendor software platform.
* Ensure functional code portability and performance portability across hardware vendors and accelerator technologies.
* Enable an extensive set of specifications and library APIs to cover programming domain needs across industries and compute as well as AI use cases.
* Meet the needs of modern software applications that merge high-end computational needs and AI.
* Provide a developer community and open forum to drive a unified API for a unified industry-wide multiarchitecture software development platform.
* Encourage ecosystem collaboration on the oneAPI specification and compatible oneAPI implementations.

## A Commitment to Open, Scalable Acceleration Freeing the Developer Ecosystem from the Chains of Proprietary Software

The oneAPI open source software platform is a major ingredient of the UXL, which is:

* A cross-industry group committed to delivering an open-standard accelerator programming model that simplifies the development of performant, cross-platform applications.
* Hosted by the Linux\* Foundation's Joint Development Foundation, which brings together ecosystem participants to establish an open standard for developing applications that deliver performance across a wide range of architectures.
* An evolution of the oneAPI software platform with its specification as its core, oneAPI and UXL use SYCL (from The Khronos Group\*) as the ISO C++ extension and abstraction layer to provide the multivendor and multiarchitecture freedom of choice at the center of their philosophy.

[UXL Foundation](https://uxlfoundation.org/)

[oneAPI Specification](https://www.oneapi.io/spec/)

[UXL Foundation/Khronos Group Announcement of SYCL for AI, HPC, and Safety-Critical Systems](https://www.khronos.org/blog/uxl-foundation-khronos-liaison-on-the-sycl-and-safety-critical-systems)

# Usher in a New Era of Accelerated AI on Intel® CPUs

Learn how Numenta\* collaborated with Intel on their Neuroscience-Based Solution to Accelerate AI Inference on CPUs. Access an implementation example with code examples.

## Get the Latest on All Things CODE

[Sign Up](https://software.seek.intel.com/developer-products-sign-up)

![author-image]()

By

**Charmaine Lai**, marketing manager, Numenta\*

This article was also published on Numenta.

## Problem Statement

Businesses across industries have witnessed the transformative potential of large language models (LLM). Despite the growing potential of LLMs, businesses still struggle to integrate LLMs into operations, mainly due to their cost, complexity, high power consumption, and concerns over data protection. GPUs have traditionally been the go-to hardware for LLMs, but they incur significant IT complications and escalating expenses that cannot sustain growing operations. Furthermore, due to worldwide demand and shortages, businesses now must wait over a year to secure GPUs for their AI projects.

## A New Approach

Numenta and Intel are setting a new precedent for LLM deployment, freeing businesses from their dependency on GPUs. The Numenta Platform for Intelligent Computing (NuPIC\*) maps neuroscience-based concepts to the Intel® Advanced Matrix Extensions (Intel® AMX) instruction set. With NuPIC, it is finally possible to deploy LLMs at scale on Intel® CPUs and deliver dramatic price/performance improvements. For examples, see benchmarks P6 and P11 in the [Performance Index for 4th Generation Intel® Xeon® Scalable Processors](https://edc.intel.com/content/www/us/en/products/performance/benchmarks/4th-generation-intel-xeon-scalable-processors/).

## Technologies

### Intel® AMX

Intel AMX accelerates matrix operations by providing dedicated hardware support (figure 1). It is particularly beneficial for applications that rely heavily on matrix computations, such as deep learning inference. Intel AMX was first introduced in 4th generation Intel® Xeon® processors and is now even better on the new 5th generation Intel Xeon processors.

Figure 1. The Intel AMX instruction set includes two key components: tiles and TMUL. Tiles are 2D units that allow parallel processing of large matrices. TMUL can perform 16 x 16 x 32 matrix multiplications in only 16 clock cycles.

### NuPIC\*

Built on a foundation of decades of neuroscience research, NuPIC allows you to build powerful language-based applications quickly and easily (figure 2). At the heart of NuPIC is a highly optimized inference server that takes advantage of Intel AMX to enable you to run LLMs efficiently on Intel CPUs. With a library of production-ready pretrained models that can be customized to a variety of natural language processing use cases, you can directly run the models in the NuPIC Inference Server. You can also fine-tune the models on your data with the NuPIC Training Module, and then deploy your custom fine-tuned model to the NuPIC Model Library and run it in the inference server.

# Developer Tools and Software for Intel® Data Center GPU Max Series

Drive breakthrough acceleration for HPC and AI workloads with the combined power of Intel® Data Center GPU Max Series and Intel® Xeon® Scalable processors—powered by oneAPI and Intel® AI developer tools.

* [Tools and Libraries](#tab-blade-1-0)
* [AI Workflows](#tab-blade-1-1)
* [HPC](#tab-blade-1-2)
* [Success Stories](#tab-blade-1-3)

### Unleash the Power of Intel Data Center GPU Max Series through Software

Intel Data Center GPU Max Series combined with oneAPI helps developers deliver high-performance, cross-architecture applications and solutions. Intel toolkits provide tools, compilers, libraries, and AI middleware to unleash hardware performance while freeing developers from proprietary environments.

#### Convenient Software Suites for AI and HPC

Accelerate AI and HPC innovation with Intel's portfolio of compilers, libraries, and tools. Intel provides the software you need to solve the world's most demanding technical challenges.

The Intel® oneAPI Base Toolkit is a starting point for heterogeneous development across CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs. It is open source, based on open standards, and features an industry-leading C++ compiler that implements SYCL\*, an evolution of C++ for heterogeneous computing. A range of performance libraries provide portable acceleration. Enhanced profiling, design assistance, and debug tools are also included.

AI Tools include additional components for data scientists and AI developers with optimizations for popular AI frameworks to run on Intel Data Center GPU Max Series for training and inference.

The Intel® oneAPI HPC Toolkit delivers what developers need to build, analyze, optimize, and scale HPC applications with the latest techniques in vectorization, multithreading, multi-node parallelization, and memory optimization. Use it to build code with Intel C++ and Fortran compilers, scale with Intel® MPI library, and analyze MPI application behavior.

## Get Started

GPU drivers must be installed first in order for the toolkits to be used on Intel Data Center GPU Max Series:

* [Linux](https://dgpu-docs.intel.com/driver/installation.html)
* Windows: not supported

* oneAPI compilers activate Intel® Xe Matrix Extensions (Intel® XMX) for acceleration.
* Intel® MPI Library activates Intel® Xe Link for faster direct GPU-to-GPU communications.

Title: Intel Xeon 6 used as Host CPUs in NVIDIA DGX Rubin NVL8 Systems
# Intel Xeon 6 used as Host CPUs in NVIDIA DGX Rubin NVL8 Systems. Intel Xeon is used as host CPU, underscoring its role to orchestrate, scale and secure modern AI infrastructure. **What’s New:** Today at NVIDIA GTC 2026, Intel announced that Intel Xeon 6 is being used as the processor for NVIDIA DGX Rubin NVL8 systems. This highlights Xeon’s role in providing architectural continuity and scalability for GPU-accelerated AI systems as workloads shift toward massive, real-time inference. AI is shifting from large-scale training to real‑time, everywhere inference—driven by agentic AI and reasoning systems. In this new era, the host CPU is mission‑critical. It governs orchestration, memory access, model security, and throughput across GPU‑accelerated systems. Intel Xeon 6 delivers leadership performance, efficiency, and compatibility with the extensive x86 software ecosystem that customers rely on to scale inference workloads. **Why It Matters:** As organizations continue to deploy AI systems, inference is increasingly defined not only by GPU throughput but also by CPU-led system performance, with the host CPU shaping overall cluster efficiency and total cost of ownership. It is also responsible for critical functions such as memory management, task orchestration, and workload distribution, while ensuring the security, reliability, and operational continuity essential to modern AI infrastructure. Building on these system-level requirements, Intel Xeon processors are used as the host CPU for DGX Rubin NVL8 systems due to their capability to support fast memory speeds, balanced performance across a range of workloads, lower long-term total cost of ownership (TCO), and their mature, enterprise-proven software ecosystem. * Optimized support throughout the ecosystem AI software stack, including new support for NVIDIA Dynamo to enable heterogeneous inference across CPU and forthcoming GPUs. This selection reinforces Intel Xeon as a cornerstone of modern AI infrastructure, enabling scalable deployment across modern data centers, the cloud and edge use cases. **About the new Intel and NVIDIA collaboration:** NVIDIA DGX Rubin NVL8 systems integrate Intel Xeon 6 processors, building on the architectural foundation established with Intel Xeon 6776P in current NVIDIA Blackwell-based platforms, including DGX B300 systems. By building on this proven foundation, Intel is helping to carry forward the performance, experience, and system-level expertise into the new DGX Rubin NVL8 systems.

AMD.overview: AMD offers datacenter AI accelerators under the Instinct brand, including the MI300X and MI300A based on CDNA 3, the MI325X, and the MI350 series built on CDNA 4 such as the MI350X, MI355X, and MI350P PCIe card, with a MI400 series planned for 2026. For client devices, AMD provides RyzenAI processors for AI PCs and workstations. Its software stack centers on ROCm, an open-source platform supporting PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX, alongside AMD Inference Microservices for enterprise AI deployment. requirements.requirement: What datacenter and client GPU/AI accelerator products does AMD offer that compete with NVIDIA GPUs, including target segments and generations?

findings.finding: AMD offers the Instinct MI300X accelerator, based on the CDNA 3 architecture, with up to 192 GB of HBM3 memory for large language model training and inference. The MI300X was sampling to key customers starting in Q3 2023. AMD also offers the Instinct MI300A, described as the world's first APU accelerator for HPC and AI workloads, which was sampling to customers.

AMD's Instinct accelerator roadmap includes the MI325X accelerator, available in Q4 2024 with up to 288 GB of HBM3E memory. The MI350 series, based on the CDNA 4 architecture, is expected to be available in 2025. The MI400 series, based on the CDNA Next architecture, is expected to arrive in 2026 for inference and large-scale AI training.

AMD Instinct MI350X and MI355X GPUs are built on the CDNA 4 architecture with 288 GB of HBM3E memory and 8 TB/s memory bandwidth. The MI350X delivers peak FP16 performance of 4.6 PFLOPS and peak FP8 performance of 9.228 PFLOPS. These air-cooled GPUs integrate with prior-generation MI300X and MI325X infrastructure.

AMD offers the Instinct MI350P PCIe card as part of the MI350 Series for deploying generative and agentic AI within existing infrastructure. The product page lists 128 GPU compute units and 144 GB of HBM3E memory. AMD positions it for leadership operating expense and simplified deployment in data centers.

AMD offers the AMD Instinct GPU as a data center AI accelerator intended for AI training and inferencing workloads. AMD positions these accelerators across deployment options that include cloud, data center, edge, and AI PCs. The Instinct accelerator is combined with EPYC CPUs and networking products for rack-scale data center AI infrastructure.

AMD's data center computing portfolio includes GPUs, AI accelerators, DPUs, SmartNICs, FPGAs, and Adaptive SoCs. These products are intended to meet computing performance requirements for data centers, supercomputers, AI and machine learning data center environments, and cloud environments.
AMD offers AMD RyzenAI processors for AI PCs and workstations. These processors support local AI experiences and responsive performance for on-device agentic AI tasks.

requirements.summary: AMD's datacenter AI accelerator portfolio includes the Instinct MI300X and MI300A based on CDNA 3, with the MI300X offering up to 192 GB of HBM3 for large language model training and inference. The roadmap extends to the MI325X with up to 288 GB of HBM3E, the CDNA 4-based MI350 series including the MI350X, MI355X, and MI350P PCIe card, and the MI400 series planned for 2026. On the client side, AMD offers RyzenAI processors for AI PCs and workstations targeting on-device agentic AI. These products serve segments spanning cloud, data center, edge, HPC, and generative or agentic AI workloads.

requirements.requirement: What software stack and developer ecosystem does AMD provide for GPU/AI computing, including framework support and adoption?

findings.finding: AMD provides ROCm, a full open-source, production-ready software stack compatible with a broad range of AMD GPUs. ROCm includes drivers, libraries, and developer tools for programming AMD GPUs and supports AI frameworks including PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX. Compatible hardware spans AMD Instinct GPUs, Radeon GPUs, and iGPUs in select Ryzen AI processors.

ROCm 7.14, released July 15, 2026, adds support for PyTorch 2.12 and JAX 0.10.0, and validates TensorFlow versions 2.21, 2.20, and 2.19.1. Transformer Engine v2.12 is validated for MI300A, MI300X, MI350X, and MI355X. The release introduces TheRock, AMD's automated open-source build and release system for ROCm.

ROCm 7.0, released September 16, 2025, provides hardware enablement for Instinct MI350X and MI355X and supports FP4, FP6, and FP8 precision formats. It includes day-0 support for PyTorch 2.7 and 2.8, TensorFlow 2.19.1, and JAX 0.6.x, along with AITER pre-optimized operators and AMD Quark production-ready models.

AMD offers AMD Inference Microservices (AIMs), described as a no licensing fee, open, standards-based enterprise-ready AI stack. AIMs is intended to simplify AI deployment and migration for generative and agentic AI workloads on AMD Instinct GPUs.

AMD provides ROCm software as part of an open, standards-based software platform. The platform is designed to enable AMD AI hardware to be deployed broadly and easily, with support for leading frameworks, cloud providers, OEMs, ISVs, and ecosystem partners.

requirements.summary: AMD provides ROCm, a full open-source production-ready software stack with drivers, libraries, and developer tools for programming AMD GPUs, supporting PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX across Instinct, Radeon, and select Ryzen AI processors. ROCm 7.0 and ROCm 7.14 added enablement for Instinct MI350X and MI355X, FP4/FP6/FP8 precision, and day-0 support for recent PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX releases. AMD also offers AMD Inference Microservices (AIMs), a no-licensing-fee enterprise-ready stack for generative and agentic AI deployment on Instinct GPUs. The platform is designed for broad deployment with cloud providers, OEMs, ISVs, and ecosystem partners.

requirements.requirement: Which customer segments and geographic markets does AMD target with its GPU and AI accelerator offerings?

findings.finding: AMD's Data Center Segment customers consist primarily of hyperscale data centers, OEMs, ODMs, system integrators, and independent distributors in domestic and international markets. Large hyperscale customers, OEMs, and ODMs deployed AMD Instinct MI350X Series GPUs in 2025. Client and Gaming Segment customers include PC OEMs, independent distributors, AIBs, and game console manufacturers.

AMD Instinct MI300X accelerators have been adopted by customers and partners including Microsoft Azure, Meta, Dell Technologies, HPE, and Lenovo. These adoptions span cloud providers and OEMs deploying AMD AI accelerators in data centers.

AMD announced in November 2026 that Neysa is scaling AI infrastructure in India with AMD Instinct, expanding access to bare-metal AI infrastructure and accelerator choice for Indian enterprises. AMD also completed the acquisition of Taalas, a specialized AI inference silicon company, in November 2026.

AMD's Instinct line of accelerators has been adopted by major cloud providers and research organizations for running large AI models. In October 2025, AMD signed a chip-supply agreement with OpenAI for OpenAI's expanding data center network. AMD also entered a $1 billion agreement with the U.S. Department of Energy to supply chips for federal high-performance computing projects.

AMD targets cloud and enterprise customers, including the world's largest hyperscale computing companies, with data center AI systems. AMD seeks to deliver end-to-end data center AI infrastructure at scale with its ecosystem for cloud and enterprise deployment.
AMD markets and sells its products directly to OEMs and through authorized third-party distributors. This distribution model applies to AMD's data center and client computing products.
AMD addresses regulated and sovereign AI, hybrid AI, edge and embedded AI, and AI PC and workstation segments. Deployment options span cloud, data center, edge, and on-device environments.

requirements.summary: AMD's Data Center Segment serves hyperscale data centers, OEMs, ODMs, system integrators, and independent distributors in domestic and international markets, with customers including Microsoft Azure, Meta, Dell Technologies, HPE, and Lenovo. Client and Gaming customers include PC OEMs, distributors, add-in board partners, and game console manufacturers. AMD also addresses regulated and sovereign AI, hybrid AI, edge and embedded AI, and AI PC and workstation segments through cloud, data center, edge, and on-device deployments. Notable engagements include infrastructure scaling in India with Neysa, a chip-supply agreement with OpenAI, and a U.S. Department of Energy high-performance computing project.

requirements.requirement: How does AMD price its datacenter GPUs and AI accelerators, and what is its enterprise go-to-market model?

findings.finding: AMD's go-to-market model includes the AMD Partner Network with Build Partners (OEMs, ODMs, hosting providers, and add-in board partners), Distributors, Solution Providers, and Embedded Partners. Sell partners include solution providers, etailers, retailers, system builders, value-added resellers, and distributors.

AMD's internal estimated pricing for an MI350P-based server is $327,238.40 USD, as cited in AMD's Advancing AI 2026 materials from July 2026. This figure is used in per-concurrency throughput-per-dollar comparisons.

AMD states the Instinct MI355X GPU hardware cost is $1.48 per hour per GPU. At a typical operating point of 129 tokens per second per user, the MI355X delivers inference at $0.173 per million tokens with 2,378 tokens per second per GPU on 24 GPUs.

AMD Inference Microservices (AIMs) is offered with no licensing fee as an open, standards-based enterprise-ready AI stack. AMD also works with cloud providers such as Vultr, which offers cloud GPU and bare-metal servers advanced by AMD Instinct GPUs and AMD EPYC CPUs.

AMD's enterprise go-to-market model emphasizes OEM go-to-market models, channel ecosystems, and enterprise infrastructure markets. AMD sells its products directly to OEMs and through authorized third-party distributors rather than exclusively through direct sales.
AMD offers AMD-based virtual machines in the cloud so customers can achieve performance and OPEX advantages. This represents a cloud consumption option for AMD GPU compute.

requirements.summary: AMD's go-to-market model uses the AMD Partner Network with Build Partners, Distributors, Solution Providers, and Embedded Partners, selling directly to OEMs and through authorized third-party distributors. Internal estimated pricing includes $327,238.40 for an MI350P-based server and $1.48 per hour per GPU for MI355X hardware, with inference cost metrics also published. AMD Inference Microservices carries no licensing fee, and AMD-based virtual machines are available in the cloud as a consumption option. The model emphasizes OEM go-to-market approaches, channel ecosystems, and enterprise infrastructure markets.

caveats: Several product availability dates are described as expected or planned rather than confirmed general availability.
Pricing figures are internal estimates cited in AMD materials and may not reflect public list prices.
Some customer and deal information relies on third-party sources with lower confidence.

Intel Corp.overview: Intel Corp offers datacenter GPU and AI accelerator products including Gaudi AI accelerators, the Data Center GPU Max Series for HPC and AI, the Data Center GPU Flex Series for virtual desktop infrastructure and visual AI, and the Arc Pro B-Series for workstations. For client systems, Intel provides Arc Graphics and Arc G-Series processors for gaming, content creation, and handheld gaming. The company supports these products with the oneAPI software stack, OpenVINO toolkit, and AI framework extensions. Intel Xeon processors with integrated AI capabilities, including Xeon 6 and 5th Generation Xeon, serve as host CPUs and handle AI inference workloads.

requirements.requirement: What datacenter GPU and AI accelerator products does Intel offer that compete with NVIDIA GPUs, including target segments and generations?

findings.finding: Intel offers Gaudi AI accelerators and Gaudi software designed for data center training and inference to bring compute advantages and choice to data center workloads.
Intel offers Data Center GPU Flex Series for virtual desktop infrastructure, media processing, and visual AI workloads.
Intel offers Arc Pro B-Series GPU for workstation performance to run larger models and process richer data.
Intel Xeon 6, Xeon 6+, and Xeon CPU Max processors are positioned for data center, network, edge, and workstation workloads.

Intel offers the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series as a datacenter GPU for HPC and AI workloads. The product is positioned as ideal for AI inference and training workflows and is deployed with Intel Xeon Scalable processors. It is powered by oneAPI and Intel AI developer tools, with oneDNN using Intel XMX to accelerate AI training and inference.

Intel offers the Intel Gaudi AI Processor as an AI accelerator for training and inferencing. Intel provides Gaudi tutorials with step-by-step instructions for running PyTorch and PyTorch Lightning models, covering beginner to advanced use cases. The tutorials support both training and inference on the Gaudi processor.

requirements.summary: Intel offers Gaudi AI accelerators and the Gaudi AI Processor for data center training and inference workloads. The Data Center GPU Max Series targets HPC and AI training and inference and is deployed with Intel Xeon Scalable processors, while the Data Center GPU Flex Series serves virtual desktop infrastructure, media processing, and visual AI workloads. The Arc Pro B-Series GPU is positioned for workstation performance to run larger models and process richer data.

requirements.requirement: What client discrete GPU products does Intel offer that compete with NVIDIA GeForce RTX, and for which segments?

findings.finding: Intel Arc Graphics are engineered for immersive gameplay, fast content creation, and easy-to-use AI capabilities.
Intel Arc G-Series processors target handheld gaming with smooth gameplay at high settings, AI-powered XeSS 3, and ray tracing.
Intel Arc A750 Graphics is part of Intel's Arc dedicated graphics family for client systems.

requirements.summary: Intel offers Arc Graphics for immersive gameplay, fast content creation, and easy-to-use AI capabilities on client systems. The Arc G-Series targets handheld gaming with high-settings gameplay, AI-powered XeSS 3, and ray tracing. The Arc A750 Graphics is part of Intel's dedicated graphics family for client systems.

requirements.requirement: What software stack and developer ecosystem does Intel provide for GPU/AI computing, including oneAPI and OpenVINO?

findings.finding: Intel oneAPI is an open, unified cross-architecture programming model supporting CPUs and accelerator architectures including GPUs and FPGAs.
Intel oneAPI includes the DPC++ Compatibility Tool for CUDA-to-SYCL code migration, enabling developers to port CUDA applications.
Intel oneAPI provides AI tools, optimized frameworks, and the OpenVINO toolkit, including oneDNN and PyTorch optimizations for Intel Core Ultra processors and Arc GPUs.
Intel released oneAPI 2025.0 tools with a standalone oneAPI HPC Toolkit and an AI Tools Selector for OpenVINO Toolkit and Gaudi AI accelerator packages.
Intel's Edge AI Portfolio combines OpenVINO for model inference, Geti platform for vision AI training, DL Streamer, and oneAPI toolkit for edge AI solutions.
Intel oneAPI offers a Unified Runtime and Codeplay plug-ins for cross-vendor GPU support.

Intel provides the oneAPI software stack through the oneAPI-samples repository, offering samples for Intel oneAPI Toolkits. The stack supports cross-architecture development across AI, CPU, GPU, FPGA, and other domains, with libraries including oneDNN, oneMKL, oneDPL, oneTBB, oneCCL, and oneDAL. Developers can use SYCL and Jupyter notebooks for AI and GPU workloads.

Intel provides the OpenVINO Toolkit as an open-source AI toolkit that enables write once, deploy anywhere inference across CPU, GPU, and NPU. The toolkit includes a model optimizer and runtime for optimizing, fine-tuning, and running AI inference. It supports AI PC development on Intel Core Ultra and Intel Core Desktop Processors, including configurations for Intel Processor Graphics and Intel NPU.

Intel provides AI framework extensions and migration tools for its GPU and CPU products. Intel Extension for PyTorch and Intel Extension for TensorFlow accelerate deep learning frameworks on Intel CPUs and GPUs. The open-source DPC++ Compatibility Tool, based on SYCLomatic, automates migration of CUDA code to SYCL for portability across architectures including Intel Data Center GPUs.

requirements.summary: Intel provides oneAPI, an open unified cross-architecture programming model supporting CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and other accelerators, with libraries such as oneDNN, oneMKL, oneDPL, oneTBB, oneCCL, and oneDAL. The stack includes the DPC++ Compatibility Tool for CUDA-to-SYCL migration, the OpenVINO Toolkit for write-once deploy-anywhere inference across CPU, GPU, and NPU, and AI framework extensions for PyTorch and TensorFlow. Intel also offers the Edge AI Portfolio combining OpenVINO, Geti, DL Streamer, and oneAPI for edge AI solutions.

requirements.requirement: How do Intel Xeon processors with integrated AI capabilities compete with NVIDIA in AI inference and CPU-plus-accelerator workloads?

findings.finding: Intel Xeon 6787P (2S) delivers 4x throughput on Speech Recognition (OpenAI Whisper) and 2.2x throughput on Computer Vision (RetinaNet) in MLPerf v5.1 inference.
Intel Xeon processors include built-in Intel AMX acceleration for higher precision ML/DL workloads.
Intel Xeon 6 processors with P-cores include Intel AMX and AVX-512 in every core, with AMX supporting INT8, BF16, and FP16 data types.
Intel Xeon processors handle AI workloads from traditional ML inference to agentic and frontier AI without GPU lock-in.
5th Generation Intel Xeon processors with Intel AMX achieved up to 17x faster BERT-Large inference in documented testing.
Intel Xeon processors serve as hosts for accelerator-dense AI systems and are available across AI systems from leading OEMs.

Intel Xeon 6 is used as the host CPU in GPU-accelerated AI systems. The host CPU governs orchestration, memory access, model security, and throughput across GPU-accelerated AI systems. It handles memory management, task orchestration, and workload distribution while supporting security, reliability, and operational continuity.

Intel Xeon 6 delivers fast memory speeds, balanced performance across a range of workloads, lower long-term total cost of ownership, and a mature enterprise-proven x86 software ecosystem. It supports scaling inference workloads across data centers, cloud, and edge use cases.

requirements.summary: Intel Xeon processors include built-in Intel AMX acceleration supporting INT8, BF16, and FP16 data types for ML/DL workloads. Xeon 6 processors with P-cores integrate AMX and AVX-512 in every core and can serve as host CPUs in GPU-accelerated AI systems, managing orchestration, memory access, and throughput. The processors handle AI workloads ranging from traditional ML inference to agentic and frontier AI, with documented MLPerf and BERT-Large inference performance results.

caveats: The verified findings do not state release status (generally available, preview, or announced) for Intel's GPU, AI accelerator, or software products.
Pricing, packaging, and regional launch timing for the Americas, Asia, and Europe are not established by the verified evidence.
Some findings describe Xeon CPUs alongside GPU and accelerator products, which may extend beyond the strict GPU/AI accelerator scope.

Department of Commerce Revises License Review Policy for Semiconductors Exported to China
— Today the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a rule revising its licensing policy for semiconductor exports to China. — Today the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a rule revising its licensing policy for semiconductor exports to China. Today’s rule follows President Trump’s December 8, 2025 announcement that the United States will allow the H200 and similar products to be shipped to approved customers in China to strengthen national security.
In order to qualify, license applicants must demonstrate that exporting these products to China will not reduce global semiconductor production capacity currently available to U.S. customers; that the Chinese purchaser has adopted export compliance procedures, including customer screening; and that the product has undergone independent, third-party testing in the United States to verify its performance and security.
